name: The Materials Project (Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory)
subcategory: computed materials-property database (DFT) and open-source tools
origin_detail: Started at DOE's Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory; Kristin Persson used Berkeley Lab LDRD seed funds in 2009 and the project launched publicly in 2011 with DOE Office of Science support. Co-founded and directed by Persson.
flagship_projects: Materials Project database and Materials API (mp-api)
MPtrj relaxation-trajectory data (used by CHGNet, MACE-MP-0, M3GNet)
openness_notes: Free registration; downloaded content offered under CC BY 4.0 (legacy terms page) and tools are open source. Since the Google DeepMind GNoME contribution, a subset of records (batch_id gnome_r2scan_statics) is access-controlled and limited to non-commercial use, so the database is no longer uniformly under one licence. Governance is a DOE-funded lab project, not a neutral foundation; scored 4 as fully open data/science infrastructure for the core.

license_history.license: GNoME r2SCAN subset: separate non-commercial terms, opt-in
license_history.note: Applies to part of the tasks, summary and materials endpoints; date of introduction not found.

risk_events: Single-sponsor dependence: funded by the DOE Office of Science (BES; also JCESR support); no annual budget is published.
Licence fragmentation after the GNoME contribution: a non-commercial subset now sits beside CC BY 4.0 data, and direct lakehouse access bypasses the API's licence controls.
robustness: Data mirrored on the AWS Open Data Registry and the platform migrated to cloud (MongoDB, AWS, Datadog) with a reported 99.98% uptime. Core codes (pymatgen) are open source and widely reused. Stewardship is still concentrated in one lab and one federal sponsor.
physical_science_relevance: The most-cited computed materials database: >200,000 inorganic materials and >577,000 molecules. Its relaxation trajectories (MPtrj) are the standard training set for universal machine-learned interatomic potentials and the Matbench Discovery benchmark. Google DeepMind used it to train initial GNoME models; Microsoft used it for MatterGen.
openness_effect_assessment: Open, free, CC BY data turned a single-lab DFT effort into shared infrastructure: users grew from >20,000 (2016) to ~120,000 (early 2020) to >650,000 (Jan 2026), and the platform has >32,000 citations. Openness also made it default AI training data for industry labs (DeepMind, Microsoft, Toyota Research Institute), which in turn contributed data back (DeepMind ~400,000 compounds) but under more restrictive terms.
key_takeaway: The Materials Project is the clearest physical-science case of government-funded open data becoming AI training infrastructure: a DOE lab project with no revenue model now underpins commercial materials-AI efforts at Google DeepMind and Microsoft. Its value is enormous in usage terms but invisible financially (no published budget), and its main risks are federal-funding dependence and creeping licence fragmentation when industry contributes data on its own terms.
